blocks.prompt: The Little Roof You Carry
blocks.text: An umbrella has bones. They are called ribs. When you push the slider up the handle, the ribs swing open like a fan and pull the cloth tight. Now you have a small roof over your head. The cloth is woven so tightly that rain cannot slip between the threads. The drops sit on top and roll off the edge. People made umbrellas for thousands of years before anyone thought to use one in the rain. In hot places, a servant held a wide umbrella over the king to keep him in the shade. That is what the name means. Umbra is an old word for shadow. Your umbrella is a little shadow you can carry with you.

3.title: The Little Roof You Carry
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8

blocks.prompt: Why an Umbrella Turns Inside Out
blocks.text: An umbrella looks simple, but it is really a small machine. A tube called the shaft runs up the middle. Thin arms called ribs hold the cloth out flat. Shorter arms called stretchers join those ribs to a ring that slides up and down the shaft. Push the ring up and the stretchers lever the ribs outward until the whole roof snaps open. Slide it back down and the umbrella folds away. On a windy day an umbrella can flip inside out, and that is not because it was built badly. Air moving across the curved top has farther to travel than the air underneath, so it moves faster and presses down less. The slower air below pushes up harder than the fast air above pushes down. That is the same lifting force that holds an airplane wing in the sky. Your umbrella is trying to fly. The ribs are made to bend instead of snap, which is why a flipped umbrella usually pops back into shape. Some umbrellas have two layers of cloth with a gap between them so the wind can spill out through the gap instead of lifting the roof.

4.title: The Little Roof You Carry
4.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: Borrowed for the Rain
blocks.text: The umbrella is one of the oldest tools people still carry every day. Carvings from ancient Egypt and Assyria, made almost three thousand years ago, show a servant walking behind a king holding a wide canopy on a pole. It was not raining in those pictures. The canopy was there to hold back the sun, and it was also a signal: the person in the shade was the person who mattered. In parts of Asia and Africa a tall parasol above someone's head meant power long before it meant weather. The words still remember this. Parasol comes from words meaning shield the sun. Umbrella grows out of the Latin word umbra, which means shade or shadow. Craftworkers in ancient China built the first umbrellas that folded, using bamboo ribs and paper stiffened with oil so water beaded and ran off instead of soaking in. Europe was slow to catch on. In eighteenth century London, a traveler named Jonas Hanway walked the streets under an umbrella in the rain and was laughed at for years. Carriage drivers shouted at him, and with reason, because a man who stays dry on foot does not pay for a ride. Hanway kept walking. Within a generation the umbrella was ordinary, and Londoners were calling one a Hanway. The frames were still heavy, built from whalebone and cane, until an English maker named Samuel Fox designed a light steel rib in 1852. The umbrella you can buy today for a few dollars is a direct descendant of his frame.

5.title: The Little Roof You Carry
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Shaft, runner, stretchers, ribs, ferrule
Whalebone and cane frames until 1852

Tightly woven cloth plus a water repellent coating
Vented double canopies resist inversion

blocks.prompt: A Machine You Can Fold
blocks.text: Almost nobody thinks of an umbrella as engineering, which is a shame, because it is one of the neatest folding structures ever put in a human hand. Run through the parts. A central shaft. A ring called the runner that slides along it. A set of long ribs that carry the cloth, and a set of shorter stretchers linking those ribs back to the runner. Every rib, stretcher, and section of shaft forms a triangle, and a triangle is the one shape that will not deform under load. Push the runner up and every triangle in the frame closes at once, forcing the ribs outward until the canopy is pulled drum tight. A spring catch takes the load, and the whole structure holds itself open with no effort from you. That is a lot of cleverness for something you leave on a bus. The fabric does its own quiet work. Rainproofing is not really about blocking water, since a single drop weighs almost nothing and falls with almost no force. It is about surface tension. The threads are woven so closely, and coated with a repellent finish, that water cannot wet the gaps between them. Instead each drop pulls itself into a bead and slides off the slope of the canopy. The umbrella does not stop the rain so much as refuse to let it stick. The frame's real enemy is not water at all. It is wind. A canopy is a curved surface with air rushing over the top of it, and curved surfaces in moving air generate lift, exactly as an aircraft wing does. Add a gust from below and an umbrella will happily turn itself inside out. Designers answer this in two ways. They make ribs from fiberglass or thin spring steel that bend and recover instead of snapping, and they cut a vent into the canopy, layering a second panel above the opening so that air escapes upward while rain still cannot fall through. It is a small solution to an old problem, and it works. Four thousand years in, the umbrella still has nothing better to replace it.

6.title: The Little Roof You Carry
6.subtitle: A reading and analysis sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: From Latin umbra, shade
Assyrian reliefs, ninth century BC
Oiled paper and bamboo in ancient China
Jonas Hanway, London, 1750s
Samuel Fox, steel Paragon rib, 1852
Hans Haupt, pocket folding Knirps, 1928
Lift, not water, is what breaks a canopy

blocks.prompt: Four Thousand Years of Shade
blocks.text: There is a rule worth remembering about inventions: the job an object was built for is often not the job it ends up doing. The umbrella is the clearest case in the world, and you can carry the evidence in one hand. Start with the name. Umbrella descends from the Latin umbra, meaning shade or shadow. Parasol is built from words meaning shield the sun. Neither word contains a single drop of water. The carvings back this up. On Assyrian palace walls from the ninth century before the common era, a servant walks behind the king holding a broad canopy on a pole, and in the dry heat of that region the point is obvious. So is the second point. Only one person in the scene is in the shade. For most of its history the umbrella was less a weather tool than a portable statement of rank, and in courts across Asia and Africa the height, color, and number of parasols above a ruler were regulated as carefully as a crown. The engineering came from the east. Chinese craftworkers built collapsible frames of bamboo, stretched paper across them, and treated the paper with oil so that water beaded and ran instead of soaking through. Once a canopy could fold, it could be personal. It could be carried by the user rather than a servant, and the object began a slow drift down the social ladder. Europe resisted anyway. In London in the 1750s a traveler named Jonas Hanway walked the streets under an umbrella in the rain and was mocked for the better part of thirty years, chiefly by carriage drivers, whose income depended on the reliable misery of wet pedestrians. Hanway won. Within a generation Londoners were asking for a Hanway by name. Then came the frames. Whalebone and cane were heavy, and they warped. In 1852 an English manufacturer named Samuel Fox patented a rib rolled from thin steel into a U shaped channel, strong along its length and light in the hand, and that single component is the reason a modern umbrella costs a few dollars instead of a week's wages. In 1928 a German engineer, Hans Haupt, added the last idea anyone has needed: a shaft that telescopes, so the whole machine collapses into a coat pocket. The physics stayed stubborn throughout. A canopy is a curved surface in moving air, and curved surfaces in moving air produce lift, which is why a gust can turn your umbrella inside out and why the thing fighting the frame is never the rain. Water is light. Wind is not. Modern answers are modest: ribs of fiberglass that bend and recover rather than break, and a vent covered by an overlapping upper panel so that air escapes while rain cannot enter. Four thousand years of refinement, and the object still does exactly what it did for an Assyrian king. It carries a small patch of shelter above one person's head. What changed is not the design. It is who gets to stand underneath.
